title: When Two Lists Mean One Thing
coreInsight: One mathematical outcome may have several descriptions or orderings; when every true outcome is represented the same number of times, divide by that multiplicity.
targetLearnerRealization: If different ordered descriptions represent the same outcome, raw counting overcounts; division is valid only when each true outcome appears the same number of times.
learningObjectives: Decide whether two ordered descriptions represent different outcomes or the same outcome.
Group duplicate descriptions and identify how many represent each true outcome.
Divide an overcount only after checking that the multiplicity is uniform.

continuity.openingCallback: Ordered lineups distinguish first from second. A team with no roles changes what counts as the same outcome.
closingSeeds: A group of three can have more than two ordered descriptions, so the duplicate factor must be found rather than guessed.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Overcounting can always be fixed by dividing by 2.
Every outcome is automatically overcounted equally often.
Different descriptions necessarily represent different mathematical outcomes.
Symmetry can be invoked without checking that the multiplicity is uniform.

beats.purpose: Reuse C3's ordered count in a setting where order no longer changes the mathematical outcome.
beats.expectedRealization: The ordered count of six describes only three teams because reversing the names does not create a new team.
beats.transitionIn: In a lineup, Ava-Ben and Ben-Ava were different. Keep that ordered count, but change the object: now the two people form a team with no roles.
beats.transitionOut: The count of six was not wrong. It counted descriptions instead of teams.
beats.whyNow: The smallest nontrivial pair selection preserves C3's 3×2 ordered count while making reversed orders visibly name the same team.
beats.entryBridge: Try the shrinking-choice count you already know, then ask what its six results actually describe.
beats.exitBridge: The six ordered name lists collapse into three pairs of descriptions.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Ordered name cards from a lineup grouped by the team they describe.
learnerPrompts: Does reversing the two names create a different team?
beats.correctFeedback: Right—there are 3 teams, even though the ordered count produces 6 descriptions.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep the ordered count. Now pair each name order with its reversal.

visual.ariaLabel: Six ordered name cards grouped into three two-person teams

steps.title: Count the descriptions
steps.body: Three choices for the first name and two for the second give six ordered name lists.

steps.title: Ask what stays the same
steps.body: Ava-Ben and Ben-Ava contain the same two people. Each team appears in exactly two name orders.

steps.title: Count the teams
steps.body: The six descriptions form three equal bundles of two.

resolution.takeaway: Before counting, decide what makes two descriptions the same outcome.

beats.purpose: Make uniform multiplicity, rather than a memorized divide-by-two move, the reason division is valid.
beats.expectedRealization: Division works because every true team has exactly two ordered descriptions.
beats.transitionIn: Look at the three bundles again. Why is dividing by 2 trustworthy here?

visual.ariaLabel: Three teams, each represented by exactly two reversed ordered descriptions

options.text: Every team has exactly two descriptions.
Every problem about pairs should be divided by 2.

feedback.six-even: An even raw count does not tell us how its descriptions are distributed among outcomes.
feedback.all-two: Exactly. Equal bundle size is what makes one division correct.
feedback.pairs-use-two: Some pair problems include repeated objects or roles, so the bundle sizes can differ.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly—each true outcome has the same multiplicity: 2.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Look inside every bundle. What shared fact do all three have?

steps.body: Division counts equal-sized bundles. If one outcome had one description and another had two, one division could not correct both.

resolution.takeaway: Find the actual multiplicity and check that it is the same for every outcome.

beats.purpose: Name overcounting and symmetry only after the learner has seen equal duplicate bundles.
beats.expectedRealization: Overcounting is corrected by dividing by a verified uniform multiplicity.
beats.transitionIn: You counted valid descriptions, then noticed that equal bundles described the same thing.
beats.name: Overcounting and symmetry
beats.conciseDefinition: Overcounting happens when several descriptions represent one outcome. Symmetry lets us divide only when every outcome has the same number of descriptions.
beats.formalization: true outcomes = descriptions ÷ descriptions per outcome
beats.memoryHook: Same thing? Same number of times? Then divide.

beats.purpose: Break the tempting always-divide-by-two rule with a tiny visible nonuniform example.
beats.expectedRealization: Mixed-flavor cups have two ordered descriptions, but double-flavor cups have only one, so 4÷2 is invalid.
beats.transitionIn: Now keep two positions, but allow the same choice twice.
beats.prompt: A two-scoop cup uses vanilla or chocolate, repeats are allowed, and scoop order does not matter. The grid has 4 ordered descriptions. Can we divide all 4 by 2?

visual.ariaLabel: A two by two grid of vanilla and chocolate ordered scoop descriptions with the mixed pair highlighted

options.text: Yes. Two scoops means divide by 2.
No. The outcomes do not all have two descriptions.

feedback.yes-two: Check VV and CC. Reversing either description produces no second grid cell.
feedback.no-unequal: Right. The mixed cup appears twice, but each double-flavor cup appears once.

beats.incorrectFeedback: Compare the diagonal cells VV and CC with the mirrored pair VC and CV.

visual.ariaLabel: Three ice cream outcomes with multiplicities one, two, and one

steps.body: There are three actual cups: vanilla-vanilla, mixed, and chocolate-chocolate.
Their description counts are 1, 2, and 1. Dividing all four ordered descriptions by 2 would incorrectly give 2 cups.

resolution.takeaway: Do not divide until every true outcome is represented equally often.

beats.purpose: Transfer paired descriptions to the approved round-robin problem, where every game appears from both teams' perspectives.
beats.expectedRealization: Team-opponent listings count every game exactly twice, so n(n−1)÷2 counts games.
beats.transitionIn: Replace each two-person team with a game between two conference teams. The same reversed pair is still one outcome.
beats.transitionOut: The division worked because every edge had exactly two endpoint descriptions—one from each team.
beats.whyNow: Every round-robin game can be listed from either team's perspective, directly scaling the paired duplicate-card structure from three people to an authentic contest setting.
beats.entryBridge: Imagine every team writing down all of its opponents. Then decide how many times one actual game enters those lists.
beats.exitBridge: Seven teams create 7×6 team-opponent descriptions, grouped two per game, for 21 games.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Ordered-pair cards collapsing into one unordered object.
learnerPrompts: Why does game A-B appear once from A's perspective and once from B's?
What equal multiplicity corrects the team-opponent count?
Are all games overcounted by the same factor?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep your choice. Count team-opponent descriptions, then pair the two descriptions of each game.

steps.title: Count from every team
steps.body: With n teams, each team lists n−1 opponents.

steps.title: Check the bundle size
steps.body: Game A-B appears on A's list and B's list. Every game appears exactly twice.

steps.title: Match 21 games
steps.body: Doubling 21 gives 42 descriptions. The consecutive factors 7 and 6 make 42, so n = 7.

resolution.takeaway: The ÷2 is justified by two endpoint descriptions per game, not by a rule that every pair problem uses 2.

beats.purpose: Harvest the invariant behind the authentic problem before independent practice.
beats.expectedRealization: A valid correction identifies the same outcome relation and verifies one common multiplicity.
beats.heading: What made the correction legal?
beats.body: We defined one game as one pair of teams. Then we checked every game had exactly two team-opponent descriptions. Only after both checks did we divide.
beats.transitionOut: On your own, name the true outcome and its multiplicity before calculating.

beats.purpose: Begin independent evidence with the two decisions that prevent blind division.
beats.heading: Your turn
beats.body: Ask two questions first: What counts as the same outcome? Does every outcome have the same number of descriptions?

beats.purpose: Check direct transfer from reversed ordered descriptions to undirected physical connections.
beats.expectedRealization: Each cord is represented by its two endpoint orders.
beats.whyNow: The physical cord makes the sameness of reversed endpoint descriptions concrete without repeating the team context.
beats.entryBridge: A cord has two endpoints. Decide whether reversing them creates a new cord.
beats.exitBridge: Twenty directed endpoint descriptions formed ten equal reversal pairs.
learnerPrompts: How many directed descriptions name each physical cord?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—10 cords connect all five pairs of beacons.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count directed endpoint descriptions, then group each one with its reversal.

steps.body: Five choices for a starting endpoint and four for a different ending endpoint give 20 directed descriptions.
A→B and B→A name the same cord, and every cord has exactly those two descriptions.

resolution.takeaway: Reversal symmetry is useful only after the two descriptions are shown to name one physical object.

beats.purpose: Check the same multiplicity with a larger roster and a different object definition.
beats.expectedRealization: Two name orders represent each role-free duet.
beats.whyNow: The learner must define a duet as an unordered outcome and verify the factor stays two as the roster grows.
beats.entryBridge: The performers have no first and second roles. What does that do to the ordered name lists?
beats.exitBridge: Thirty ordered name lists became fifteen two-description bundles.
learnerPrompts: Would reversing the two musicians change the performance?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Start with 6×5 ordered lists and check how many describe each duet.

steps.body: The ordered name count is 6×5 = 30.
Every duet appears in exactly two orders, so 30÷2 = 15.

resolution.takeaway: The roster changed, but the two-description symmetry did not.

beats.purpose: Mix C3 factorial counting with duplicate descriptions created by identical objects.
beats.expectedRealization: Temporarily labeling identical objects creates two descriptions of every visible arrangement.
beats.whyNow: This reconnects to factorial arrangements while changing the symmetry from reversing a pair to swapping temporary labels on identical objects.
beats.entryBridge: Use the factorial count from ordered lineups—but watch what happens if the two identical red flags are temporarily labeled.
beats.exitBridge: Swapping the two red labels paired all 120 labeled rows into 60 visible rows.
learnerPrompts: How many labeled rows collapse to one visible row after the red subscripts are erased?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Label the red flags R₁ and R₂, count all five distinct flags, then erase the labels.

visual.ariaLabel: A factorial count of labeled flags grouped in pairs that differ only by swapping the two red labels

steps.body: Treating R₁, R₂, blue, green, and yellow as distinct gives 5! = 120 labeled rows.
Every visible row has exactly two labeled versions, formed by swapping R₁ and R₂.

resolution.takeaway: A symmetry can be a label swap as well as a reversal; the same uniform-multiplicity check still controls the division.

beats.purpose: Require the learner to repair a nonuniform overcount rather than apply one global division.
beats.expectedRealization: Repeated-flavor and mixed-flavor outcomes must be handled separately because their multiplicities differ.
beats.whyNow: This is the independent version of the lesson's counterexample and makes choosing the correct representation more important than repeating a calculation.
beats.entryBridge: This time there are four flavors. Check the diagonal and off-diagonal descriptions before deciding whether one division works.
beats.exitBridge: The four double-flavor outcomes stayed single while the twelve mixed descriptions paired into six outcomes.
learnerPrompts: Which outcomes have one description, and which have two?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Do not divide all 16 ordered descriptions at once. Separate repeated-flavor cups from mixed cups.

visual.ariaLabel: Two kinds of ice cream outcomes separated by multiplicity one and multiplicity two

steps.body: The four same-flavor cups lie on the grid's diagonal and each has one description.
The twelve mixed descriptions pair with their reversals, giving 12÷2 = 6 mixed cups.
Add the two kinds.

resolution.takeaway: When multiplicity is not uniform, separate the outcomes into parts where it is uniform.

beats.purpose: Check authentic transfer where home/away changes which reversed descriptions are distinct outcomes.
beats.expectedRealization: Home and away turn the two orders of a team pair into two actual games, so the conference ledger should not be divided twice.
beats.whyNow: The additional mapped bank problem tests whether the learner defines the true outcome before dividing: home-versus-away order matters, while the two team perspectives on one scheduled game still do not.
beats.entryBridge: Read carefully: one matchup now creates a home game and an away game. Decide which reversals are duplicates and which are genuinely different games.
beats.exitBridge: The 28 unordered matchups produced 56 distinct home/away games, then 32 outside games brought the total to 88.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Ordered-pair cards checked against the problem's definition of one game.
learnerPrompts: Why does the pairing board use only one triangle?
Which two distinct games come from each conference matchup?
Why is each outside game counted once for a Middle School Eight team?
Which two disjoint game ledgers combine at the end?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct—88 games involve the conference teams.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Separate conference games from outside games, and check whether home-away creates duplicates or distinct games.

steps.title: Count conference matchups once
steps.body: The 8×7 ordered team descriptions pair by reversal, giving 8×7÷2 = 28 matchups.

steps.title: Restore home and away
steps.body: Each matchup creates two genuinely different games, so 28×2 = 56 conference games.

steps.title: Count outside games
steps.body: Each of the 8 conference teams plays 4 non-conference games. Those opponents are outside the conference, so no such game belongs to two conference-team schedules.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: Conference and non-conference games are disjoint.

resolution.takeaway: Whether reversal creates a duplicate depends on what the problem calls one outcome. Home-away order matters here.

beats.purpose: Consolidate sameness, actual multiplicity, and uniformity before opening the successor tension.
beats.expectedRealization: All three checks are required before dividing an overcount.
beats.transitionIn: Before the group size changes, keep the checks that made every correction trustworthy.
beats.prompt: Which checks must happen before dividing an overcount? Select all three.

options.text: Define when descriptions mean the same outcome.
Find how many descriptions represent each outcome.
Check that this number is the same for every outcome.
Use 2 whenever the objects come in pairs.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Same outcome, actual multiplicity, uniform multiplicity.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The correction factor comes from the descriptions, not from a keyword such as pair.

groups.label: 1. Same outcome?
choices: decide what order or labels change

visual.ariaLabel: Three-part checklist for correcting an overcount

resolution.takeaway: Do not guess the divisor. Prove the bundle size.

beats.purpose: Change pairs to three-person groups and leave the larger multiplicity unresolved for C7.
beats.expectedRealization: A three-person group has several ordered lineups, so a systematic way to remove order is needed.
beats.transitionIn: Now change one feature: choose three people for a role-free group, but count them first as an ordered lineup.
beats.prompt: ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, and CBA all use the same three people. For a larger roster, how could we remove all those artificial orders without listing every group?
beats.takeaway: The same group can hide behind several lineups—not just two. Next we will turn that duplicate structure into a general way to choose without order.

notes: Draft connector authored with the repo-local mathinking-lesson Skill.
The generated three-person example is preferred for discovery because it isolates duplicate ordered descriptions before the authentic round-robin arithmetic.
The lesson uses existing generic primitives and the approved bank animation; no lesson-specific renderer behavior was added.
The nonuniform ice-cream example explicitly blocks an always-divide-by-two rule before final practice.
